title: Affordance
desc: A signal that tells the user what action is possible — without needing instruction.
body:
An affordance is a property of an object or interface element that communicates how it should be used. A door handle affords pulling. A button affords pressing. The concept was introduced by psychologist James Gibson and later applied to design by Don Norman in The Design of Everyday Things.

In digital interfaces, affordances are mostly visual — a raised button looks pressable, an underlined word looks clickable. When affordances are missing or misleading, users hesitate, make errors, or give up.

**Why it matters:** Every time a user has to stop and think 'can I click this?', an affordance has failed. Good affordances make the right action feel obvious.

**Example:** A text input field with a visible border and a blinking cursor affords typing. A flat label with no border does not — even if it is technically editable.

title: Cognitive load
desc: The mental effort required to process and use an interface. Less is almost always better.
body:
Cognitive load refers to the total amount of mental effort a user has to exert to understand and operate an interface. It comes from cognitive psychology — specifically John Sweller's work in the 1980s — and has become a foundational principle in UX design.

There are three types: intrinsic load (the inherent complexity of the task), extraneous load (complexity added by poor design), and germane load (effort that builds useful mental models). Good design reduces extraneous load.

**Why it matters:** Users have a limited mental bandwidth. Every unnecessary decision, label, animation, or option consumes some of it. When cognitive load is too high, users make mistakes, feel frustrated, or abandon the task entirely.

**Example:** A form that asks for 12 fields when 4 would do, uses jargon in its labels, and shows all error messages at once has high cognitive load. A form that shows one question at a time, uses plain language, and validates inline has low cognitive load.

title: Mental model
desc: The internal picture a user builds of how a system works — not how it actually works.
body:
A mental model is the internal representation a person builds in their head of how something works. It is based on past experience, analogies, and observation — not on technical reality. Users interact with your interface based on their mental model, not yours.

The job of a UX designer is to understand users' existing mental models and either design to match them, or help users build accurate new ones.

**Why it matters:** When an interface violates a user's mental model, confusion follows. If your app calls something a 'workspace' but the user thinks of it as a 'project', they will struggle to find things — even if the functionality is identical.

**Example:** Most users have a mental model of email as a physical letter — it goes to one person, it sits in a inbox, you reply to it. Designers of early email apps leaned into this metaphor deliberately. Slack challenged it by introducing channels, which required users to build a new mental model.

title: Role prompting
desc: Priming the AI with a persona to shape its tone and level of expertise.
body:
Role prompting means opening your prompt by assigning the AI a specific identity or expertise. This shapes how it frames its response — the vocabulary it uses, the assumptions it makes, the depth it goes to.

The pattern looks like: 'You are a [role] with expertise in [domain]. [Your actual request].'

**Why it matters:** A general question gets a general answer. The same question asked of 'a senior UX designer who has worked on enterprise SaaS products for 10 years' gets a more specific, more useful answer — because the model adjusts its framing to match the persona.

**Example:**
- Weak: 'How should I design this form?'
- Strong: 'You are a UX designer specialising in reducing form abandonment. Review this checkout flow and identify the three highest-friction points.'

**Watch out for:** Overloading the role with too many attributes. One clear, specific role works better than 'you are a world-class expert genius designer researcher developer'.

title: Chain of thought
desc: Asking the model to reason step by step before giving a final answer.
body:
Chain of thought prompting instructs the AI to show its reasoning process before arriving at a conclusion. Rather than jumping straight to an answer, the model works through intermediate steps — which tends to produce more accurate and more trustworthy outputs.

The simplest version is appending 'Think step by step' to your prompt. More deliberate versions ask the model to outline its reasoning, identify assumptions, or consider alternatives before concluding.

**Why it matters:** For complex problems — logic, analysis, multi-step decisions — an AI that skips straight to an answer is more likely to be confidently wrong. Showing the reasoning lets you spot where it went off track.

**Example:**
- Without: 'Which of these two designs is better?'
- With: 'Compare these two designs step by step — first evaluate information hierarchy, then visual clarity, then likely user behaviour. Then give your recommendation.'

**Related:** This is one of the most well-researched prompting techniques. It consistently improves performance on reasoning tasks.

title: Information hierarchy
desc: The visual order in which content is presented to guide the user's eye.
body:
Information hierarchy is the deliberate organisation of visual elements so that the most important information is noticed first, and secondary information follows in a logical order. It is created through size, weight, colour, contrast, spacing and position.

A strong hierarchy means a user can scan a page in seconds and understand what it is, what the key actions are, and where to look next. A weak hierarchy makes everything feel equally important — which means nothing stands out.

**Why it matters:** Users don't read interfaces, they scan them. Hierarchy is what makes scanning work. Without it, cognitive load increases and users miss key information.

**Example:** On this page, the entry title is large and serif — it demands attention first. The type label is small, uppercase and ochre — it provides context without competing. The description is smaller and muted — it rewards closer reading. That ordering is hierarchy in action.

title: Context window
desc: The amount of text an AI can hold in working memory at once — your conversation has a limit.
body:
The context window is the total amount of text — measured in tokens — that an AI model can process in a single interaction. Everything the model can 'see' at once lives inside this window: your system prompt, the conversation history, any documents you've shared, and the response it is generating.

When a conversation exceeds the context window, older content gets dropped. The model doesn't remember it — it genuinely cannot see it anymore.

**Why it matters:** Long conversations with heavy context can start to degrade. The model may seem to 'forget' earlier instructions or lose consistency. Understanding the context window helps you structure conversations and prompts more effectively.

**Practical implications:**
- Front-load critical instructions — don't bury them deep in a long thread
- Summarise and restart long conversations rather than letting them run indefinitely
- When using AI for code, paste only the relevant file — not your entire codebase

**Tokens vs words:** Roughly 1 token ≈ 0.75 words in English. A 200,000 token context window holds around 150,000 words — about two full novels.

title: Semantic HTML
desc: Using the right HTML element for what it represents, not just how it looks.
body:
Semantic HTML means choosing HTML elements based on their meaning — what the content is — rather than their default visual appearance. A heading is a `<h1>`, not a `<div>` styled to look big. A navigation is a `<nav>`, not a `<div class='nav'>`. A button is a `<button>`, not a `<div>` with an onClick.

**Why it matters:** Semantic HTML communicates structure to browsers, search engines, and assistive technologies like screen readers. A screen reader knows that a `<nav>` contains navigation links and can skip to it. It has no idea what a `<div class='nav'>` means.

It also affects SEO — search engines use semantic structure to understand what a page is about and rank it accordingly.

**Common mistakes:**
- Using `<div>` for everything instead of `<article>`, `<section>`, `<aside>`, `<header>`, `<footer>`
- Using `<span>` or `<div>` as buttons because they are easier to style
- Skipping heading levels (going from `<h1>` straight to `<h4>`)

**Example:** On Scaffold, each knowledge entry is semantically an `<article>`. The site title is an `<h1>`. The filter buttons are real `<button>` elements. None of this affects how it looks — but it makes the site accessible and meaningful to machines.

title: Negative constraints
desc: Telling the AI what not to do can be as powerful as telling it what to do.
body:
Negative constraints are explicit instructions about what the AI should avoid in its response. They work alongside positive instructions to narrow the output space — ruling out directions you don't want before the model starts generating.

The pattern is simple: after stating what you want, add a line beginning with 'Do not...' or 'Avoid...' or 'Do not include...'.

**Why it matters:** AI models default to common patterns. Without constraints, you get the most average, expected version of what you asked for. Negative constraints push the model away from defaults and toward more specific, intentional output.

**Example:**
- 'Write a short description of this feature. Do not use the words innovative, seamless, or powerful. Do not use exclamation marks. Do not write more than two sentences.'

All three constraints rule out common AI writing habits — and the result is almost always tighter and more human.

**Related:** Negative constraints are especially useful when you have been burned by a specific bad pattern before. If the AI keeps doing something you don't want, name it explicitly.

title: MCP / tool use
desc: A protocol that lets AI agents connect to external services and take real-world actions.
body:
Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open standard that allows AI models to connect to external tools and services — giving them the ability to take actions beyond generating text. Through MCP, an AI can search the web, read files, query databases, send emails, update calendars, and more.

Tool use more broadly refers to any mechanism that lets a model call an external function and incorporate the result into its response. MCP is one standardised implementation of this idea.

**Why it matters:** Without tool use, an AI is limited to its training data and your conversation. With tool use, it becomes an agent — something that can interact with the world on your behalf.

**How it works (simplified):**
1. A tool is described to the model — its name, what it does, and what inputs it needs
2. When the model decides a tool is relevant, it outputs a structured call
3. The tool runs and returns a result
4. The model incorporates the result into its response

**Example:** When Claude searches the web in this conversation, that is tool use. When Claude reads a file you uploaded, that is tool use. MCP makes these integrations standardised so any compatible tool can connect to any compatible model.

title: Zero-shot prompting
desc: Asking an AI to complete a task without giving it any examples of what a good answer looks like.
body:
**What it means**

Zero-shot means you give the model zero examples before asking your question. You just describe the task and trust the model to figure out the format, tone, and approach on its own.

This is actually how most people use AI by default — you ask a question, you get an answer.

**When it works well**

- Simple, well-defined tasks ("Summarise this paragraph")
- Tasks the model has seen a lot during training (writing, translation, explanation)
- When you want a quick result and don't need a specific format

**When it falls short**

If you need output in a very specific structure — a particular JSON shape, a formatted table, a certain writing voice — zero-shot often produces something close but not quite right. That's when few-shot prompting becomes useful: you show the model exactly what you want before asking for it.

title: Few-shot prompting
desc: Giving an AI one or more examples of the output you want before asking it to produce something new.
body:
**What it means**

Instead of just describing what you want, you show the model. You provide one, two, or three examples of an ideal input-output pair, then ask the model to follow the same pattern for a new input.

**A simple example**

If you wanted the model to rewrite product names in a punchy two-word style, you might write:

- Input: Running shoes → Output: Swift Stride
- Input: Coffee maker → Output: Dawn Brew
- Input: Yoga mat → Output: ...

The model now understands the format, the tone, and the length you want — without you having to describe any of it.

**Why it works**

Models are very good at pattern recognition. Examples are often clearer than instructions. Showing beats telling.

**Practical tip**

You only need 1–3 examples in most cases. More than that rarely improves results and just uses up context.

title: Role prompting
desc: Telling an AI to take on a specific role or persona to shape the tone, depth, and framing of its response.
body:
**What it means**

You open your prompt by assigning the model an identity — "You are a senior UX designer," "You are a plain-language editor," "You are a sceptical code reviewer." This primes the model to respond from that perspective.

**Why it helps**

The same question answered by a "junior copywriter" and a "brand strategist with 20 years of experience" will produce meaningfully different responses. The role sets expectations for vocabulary, depth of reasoning, and what the model chooses to prioritise.

**Where it's most useful**

- Getting expert-level framing on a topic you don't know well
- Setting a consistent tone across a long working session
- Getting critical feedback — "You are a harsh but fair editor" produces more useful critique than just asking for a review

**Limitation**

Role prompting influences style and framing, but it doesn't give the model knowledge it doesn't have. Assigning it the role of a cardiologist won't make its medical output more accurate — it will just sound more medical.

title: Chain-of-thought prompting
desc: Asking an AI to reason through a problem step by step before giving its final answer, which tends to produce more accurate results.
body:
**What it means**

Instead of asking for an answer directly, you ask the model to show its work — to think out loud before concluding. The simplest version is adding "think step by step" to your prompt.

**Why it improves accuracy**

Language models generate text token by token. When forced to reason through intermediate steps, each step becomes context for the next one. This matters most for tasks involving logic, maths, multi-step decisions, or anything where jumping straight to an answer leads to errors.

**Example**

Without chain-of-thought: "Which of these three options has the lowest total cost?" — the model might just guess.

With chain-of-thought: "Think through the cost of each option step by step, then tell me which is lowest." — the model works through each one in sequence, making errors much less likely.

**When to use it**

- Any task involving numbers or logic
- Decisions with multiple factors to weigh
- When you want to check the model's reasoning, not just accept its conclusion
- Debugging — "Walk me through what this code does line by line"

title: Context window
desc: The maximum amount of text an AI model can hold in its working memory at one time — everything it can see and reason about in a single conversation.
body:
**What it means**

Every AI model has a context window — a fixed upper limit on how much text it can process at once. This includes your messages, the model's replies, any documents you paste in, and system instructions. Once you hit the limit, the model can no longer see the earliest parts of the conversation.

**Why it matters for prompting**

If you're working on a long task — refining a document across many turns, debugging a large codebase, maintaining a complex conversation — the context window is your constraint. As the conversation grows, older context falls away.

**Practical implications**

- Paste only the relevant parts of a document, not the whole thing
- For long projects, periodically summarise what's been decided so key context stays present
- Starting a new conversation resets the window — useful when a thread has become cluttered

**A useful mental model**

Think of it as a desk. The model can only work with what's on the desk right now. The longer the conversation, the more gets pushed off the back edge.

title: Affordance
desc: A visual property of an element that suggests how it should be used — a button looks pressable, a slider looks draggable.
body:
**Origin**

The term was coined by psychologist James Gibson and popularised in design by Don Norman in The Design of Everyday Things. Norman used it to describe the perceived — not just actual — properties of an object that tell you how to interact with it.

**In digital interfaces**

Affordances are mostly visual cues. A rectangular shape with a subtle shadow looks like a button you can press. Underlined blue text looks like a link you can click. A horizontal bar with a handle looks draggable.

Good affordances mean users don't need to think — they just act.

**When affordances fail**

Flat design trends (lots of white space, minimal borders, ghost buttons) have made affordances harder to read. If a button looks identical to plain text, users may not realise it's interactive.

**Perceived vs actual affordance**

- Perceived affordance: what the user thinks the element can do
- Actual affordance: what it can really do

The gap between these two is where confusion lives. A door with a pull handle that you have to push is the classic example — the handle affords pulling, but the mechanism requires pushing.

title: Visual hierarchy
desc: The arrangement of elements so the eye naturally moves from most important to least important, using size, weight, colour, and spacing as guides.
body:
**What it means**

Visual hierarchy is the invisible order a design imposes on the viewer's attention. Without it, everything fights for focus equally — which means nothing gets seen first. With it, the eye has a clear path.

**The main tools**

- **Size** — larger elements read first. A big headline dominates a small caption.
- **Weight** — bold text reads before regular text at the same size.
- **Colour** — high contrast and accent colours draw the eye before neutral grey.
- **Spacing** — isolated elements feel more important than crowded ones.
- **Position** — top-left reads before bottom-right in most Western layouts.

**A practical test**

Squint at your design until it blurs. What you can still make out is your hierarchy. If the wrong things survive the squint test, the hierarchy needs work.

**In Scaffold's design system**

This is active in every card: the ochre type label pulls the eye first (colour contrast), the serif title comes next (size and weight), the mono description follows (smaller, grey), and the tag pill reads last (smallest, border only). Each layer has a clear rank.

title: Mental model
desc: The internal picture a user carries of how a system works — often incomplete or wrong, but the reality designers have to design for.
body:
**What it means**

A mental model is what a user believes about how something works. It's built from past experience, analogies, and guesswork. It's rarely a perfect match for how the system actually works — but it's what they'll use to make decisions.

**Why it matters**

When a design matches the user's mental model, it feels intuitive. When it doesn't, friction appears — the user clicks the wrong thing, gets confused, or gives up.

**A classic example**

Early users of cloud storage often imagined files still living on their computer and being copied to the cloud. When they deleted a file locally and it disappeared from cloud storage too, they were surprised — because their mental model said the cloud was a separate backup, not a sync.

**Designing for mental models**

You have two options: match the user's existing mental model, or change it. Matching is almost always cheaper. Changing requires clear onboarding, good error messages, and patience.

**Useful question to ask**

What does the user think will happen when they do this action? If your answer doesn't match what actually happens, you have a design problem.

title: Fitts's Law
desc: A principle stating that the time to click a target depends on how large it is and how far away it is — bigger and closer means faster.
body:
**The idea**

Fitts's Law is a predictive model from 1954 that holds up surprisingly well in digital design. It says: the time to move to and click a target is a function of the target's size and the distance to it. Bigger targets and shorter distances = faster, easier interaction.

**Practical design implications**

- Make buttons large enough to hit comfortably — especially on mobile where fingers are imprecise
- Place frequently used controls close to where the user already is
- Screen edges and corners are effectively infinite targets (you can't overshoot them) — which is why macOS puts the menu bar at the very top edge of the screen
- Destructive actions (delete, remove) should be smaller or further away — friction is protective here

**On mobile specifically**

Fitts's Law becomes critical on touch interfaces. The minimum comfortable tap target is generally considered 44×44px. Anything smaller creates frustration, especially for users with larger fingers or motor impairments.

**The takeaway**

If users are missing a button, making it bigger or moving it closer will fix the problem faster than changing its label.

title: Feedback (UI)
desc: The system's way of telling the user that something happened — a confirmation, a state change, or an error — so they know their action was received.
body:
**What it means**

Feedback is the interface talking back. Every time a user does something — clicks, submits, deletes, saves — they need to know it worked. Without feedback, users are left guessing, and guessing leads to repeated actions, anxiety, and distrust.

**Forms of feedback**

- **Visual** — a button changes colour when pressed, a spinner appears while loading, a form field turns red on error
- **Textual** — "Your changes have been saved", "Invalid email address"
- **Motion** — a list item slides out when deleted, a modal shakes when you try to dismiss without completing a required field
- **Haptic** — a vibration on mobile when an action completes or fails

**The feedback loop**

Good interfaces follow a simple loop: user acts → system responds → user understands result → user acts again. Breaking any part of that loop creates confusion.

**Common failures**

- A button that doesn't visually respond to being clicked (did it register?)
- A form that submits and nothing happens (did it work?)
- An error message that says "Something went wrong" with no guidance on what to do next

**Response timing matters**

Feedback needs to feel connected to the action. Anything over ~100ms for a visual response starts to feel laggy. Anything over 1 second needs a loading indicator.
